entities.summary:
Servius Sulpicius Galba, born 3 BCE and assassinated 15 January 69 CE, was a Roman senator and general who briefly served as emperor from 8 June 68 CE until his violent overthrow. His ascension marked the end of the Julio-Claudian dynasty and plunged the Roman Empire into the tumultuous "Year of the Four Emperors," a period of civil war that profoundly challenged the stability of the imperial succession. Galba's reign, though short, revealed the fragility of the principate when an emperor lacked military support and a clear succession plan, paving the way for a new era of military-backed emperors.

Galba's path to power began in Hispania Tarraconensis, where he served as governor and openly rebelled against Emperor Nero in April 68 CE, capitalizing on widespread discontent among the legions and the Praetorian Guard. With the support of figures like Otho and the defection of the Praetorian Prefect Nymphidius Sabinus, Nero's authority collapsed, leading to his suicide on 9 June 68 CE. Galba entered Rome on 11 October 68 CE, but his austere policies, including the cancellation of Nero's lavish gifts to the army, his perceived avarice, and his execution of several prominent figures without trial, quickly alienated key power brokers, particularly the Praetorian Guard and the legions on the Rhine frontier.

The widespread dissatisfaction culminated in the legions in Germania Superior refusing to swear loyalty to Galba on 1 January 69 CE and instead proclaiming Vitellius as emperor. In Rome, Galba's adoption of Lucius Calpurnius Piso Frugi Licinianus as his successor, bypassing his early supporter Otho, proved to be a fatal miscalculation. Otho swiftly instigated a coup with the Praetorian Guard, leading to Galba's assassination in the Roman Forum on 15 January 69 CE, after a reign of just seven months and seven days. His death ignited the first major civil war since the end of the Roman Republic, directly leading to the reigns of Otho and Vitellius.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Galba's brief but violent reign directly triggered the 'Year of the Four Emperors,' the first major civil war since the Republic, and profoundly demonstrated that military support, not just dynastic legitimacy, was essential for Roman imperial power. His death paved the way for the Flavian dynasty and reshaped the nature of imperial succession.
